title: Pacific nations reassure Beijing, Canberra’s treaties aren’t exclusive
gist: Within a week of the Australia–PNG Pukpuk Treaty taking legal effect, Port Moresby ordered Taiwan's representative office closed and China publicly commended it — the latest case of Pacific states signing with Canberra then immediately reassuring Beijing. The author's structural point: security treaties are not exclusivity clauses, and Nauru, Vanuatu and now PNG have each demonstrated that, with LNG trade to Taiwan (40% of PNG exports, a third going to Taipei) the concrete asset at risk.

insights.claim: Papua New Guinea ordered Taiwan's representative office in Port Moresby to close just days after the Pukpuk Treaty, its bilateral alliance with Australia, came into legal effect — signalling to Beijing within a week of its most important security agreement that the China door stays open.
insights.speaker: Connor Graham
insights.so_what: Signing a security pact with Canberra does not buy alignment; expect immediate offsetting gestures to Beijing after each new Australian agreement.
insights.locator: The sudden closure comes just days after the Pukpuk Treaty

insights.claim: A security treaty is not an exclusivity clause on the relationship, and Pacific nations have made clear they do not intend to treat it as one.
insights.speaker: Connor Graham
insights.so_what: The core analytical frame: Australian treaty wins should not be read as Chinese exclusion — the influence contest continues after signature.
insights.quote: But a security treaty is not an exclusivity clause on the relationship – and Pacific nations have made it clear they do not intend to treat it as one.
insights.locator: But a security treaty is not an exclusivity clause

insights.claim: PNG's move is the latest evidence of what Foreign Minister Penny Wong calls the "permanent contest" for influence in the Pacific, even after recent Australian diplomatic successes.
insights.speaker: Connor Graham
insights.so_what: Frames Pacific influence as an ongoing recurring-cost commitment for Canberra, not a series of closable wins — relevant to sustained aid and defence budget lines.
insights.locator: PNG's actions are the latest evidence

insights.claim: PNG Foreign Minister Justin Tkatchenko framed the Taiwan office closure as routine adherence to PNG's one-China policy, timed to the 50th anniversary of PNG–China diplomatic relations, while Taiwan called the decision unilateral and without consultation or warning.
insights.speaker: Connor Graham
insights.so_what: The 'routine administrative' framing is the deniability device that makes these closures low-cost — expect the same language elsewhere.
insights.locator: Foreign Minister Justin Tkatchenko framed it

insights.claim: China's foreign ministry "highly commended" the closure before reaffirming the comprehensive strategic partnership with PNG, while an unnamed US State Department spokesperson called it "yet another example of Beijing's intimidation campaign".
insights.speaker: Connor Graham
insights.so_what: Public Chinese reward plus US verbal condemnation with no cost imposed shows the incentive structure favours further defections.
insights.quote: yet another example of Beijing’s intimidation campaign
insights.locator: China's foreign ministry "highly commended" the move

insights.claim: Taipei has announced it will review its trade with PNG following the office closure, with the review centring on liquefied natural gas exports from PNG to Taiwan.
insights.speaker: Connor Graham
insights.so_what: A live LNG offtake review is the tradeable consequence of the diplomatic move — watch PNG LNG contract reallocation.
insights.locator: Taipei has announced it will review its trade with PNG

insights.claim: LNG makes up an estimated 40% of PNG's total exports, amounting to US$5.36 billion in 2024, and around a third of those LNG exports go to Taiwan.
insights.speaker: Connor Graham
insights.so_what: Quantifies PNG's concentration risk — roughly 13% of total exports ride on a single buyer now reviewing the relationship.
insights.locator: For PNG, LNG makes up an estimated 40% of total exports

insights.claim: PNG's LNG supplies comprise only approximately 6% of Taiwan's LNG imports, a shortfall that may be readily absorbed by Australia, Qatar and the United States, which already supply the bulk of Taiwan's LNG.
insights.speaker: Connor Graham
insights.so_what: The asymmetry favours Taiwan: substitution is easy for Taipei, painful for Port Moresby — potential incremental volume for Australian, Qatari and US suppliers.
insights.locator: comprising only approximately 6% of Taiwan's LNG imports

insights.claim: Despite the asymmetric trade exposure, PNG appears to have deemed strengthening its relationship with Beijing more critical than damaging relations with Taipei — revealing a political preference that overrides near-term export economics.
insights.speaker: Connor Graham
insights.so_what: Economic-cost arguments are not deterring Pacific alignment shifts; model these decisions on political and investment-promise logic instead.
insights.locator: But PNG appears to have deemed strengthening its relationship with Beijing

insights.claim: China's trade with PNG exceeded K17 billion (US$4.4 billion) in 2024 with a surplus of more than K7 billion (US$1.9 billion) in PNG's favour, according to China's ambassador to PNG Yang Xiaoguang.
insights.speaker: Connor Graham
insights.so_what: A trade balance running in PNG's favour gives Beijing a durable economic argument that Taipei cannot match.
insights.locator: China's trade with PNG exceeded K17 billion

insights.claim: Prime Minister James Marape spent three days in Guangzhou in April discussing mining and energy deals that could exceed the value of PNG–Taiwan trade in the long run, and a PNG–China free trade agreement is under consideration.
insights.speaker: Connor Graham
insights.so_what: Prospective mining and energy deal value is the actual consideration being paid for diplomatic alignment — track whether the deals materialise.
insights.locator: In April this year, Prime Minister James Marape spent three days in Guangzhou

insights.claim: The December 2024 Nauru-Australia Treaty gave Canberra effective veto power over Nauru's dealings with other countries in security, banking and telecommunications in exchange for A$100 million in budget support and A$40 million for policing over five years.
insights.speaker: Connor Graham
insights.so_what: Sets the observable market price of a Pacific security veto — roughly A$140 million over five years for a microstate.
insights.locator: The December 2024 Nauru-Australia Treaty

insights.claim: Eight months after signing that treaty, Nauru's foreign minister signed an investment proposal worth approximately A$1 billion with Chinese state-linked company China-CRRDC, announced by media release before any consultation with Australian officials, and Canberra flagged it as potentially contravening the treaty.
insights.speaker: Connor Graham
insights.so_what: A billion-dollar Chinese proposal dwarfs Australia's A$140m package — Canberra's veto rights are being tested by an order-of-magnitude bid.
insights.locator: Eight months later, Nauru's foreign minister signed an investment proposal

insights.claim: Nauru's government has ordered all personnel representing its government and state-owned enterprises, in-country and abroad, to observe the one-China principle, a clear reaffirmation of alignment to Beijing.
insights.speaker: Connor Graham
insights.so_what: Formal one-China directives inside state-owned enterprises indicate alignment is being embedded operationally, not just declared.
insights.locator: Nauru's government has also ordered

insights.claim: Little is known publicly about China-CRRDC, the Chinese state-linked counterparty to Nauru's roughly A$1 billion investment proposal.
insights.speaker: Connor Graham
insights.so_what: Counterparty opacity is itself a signal — deal execution risk is high and diligence on Pacific Chinese investment vehicles is thin.
insights.locator: Little is known about the company involved

themes.theme: Vanuatu and Fiji: veto rights negotiated down

insights.claim: Vanuatu's original Nakamal Agreement with Australia, due for signing in September 2025, was renegotiated over concerns it would hand Australia veto power over Vanuatu's third-party engagement, and only a watered-down version with consultation rather than full veto rights was signed in June 2026.
insights.speaker: Connor Graham
insights.so_what: Veto clauses are becoming unsellable in the Pacific — future Australian agreements will likely carry weaker exclusion provisions.
insights.locator: In Vanuatu, the original Nakamal Agreement with Australia

insights.claim: Throughout the Nakamal renegotiation, Vanuatu simultaneously engaged Beijing on its own comprehensive agreement known as Namele, ensuring its commitment to Australia would not read in Beijing as a rejection of China.
insights.speaker: Connor Graham
insights.so_what: Parallel-track negotiation with both powers is now standard Pacific practice — assume any Australian deal has a Chinese counterpart in progress.
insights.locator: But, throughout the renegotiation process, Vanuatu also engaged with Beijing

insights.claim: Australia signed a landmark alliance with Fiji (Veitacini) alongside a comprehensive agreement (Vuvale) earlier this month, capping a "hot streak" of Pacific diplomacy for the Albanese government and firming Australia's position as the region's security partner of choice.
insights.speaker: Connor Graham
insights.so_what: Australia has genuinely won the security-partner slot; the open question is whether that converts to any exclusion of Chinese economic influence.
insights.locator: Earlier this month, Australia signed a landmark alliance with Fiji

insights.claim: Maintaining Australia's position as the Pacific's partner of choice will require the same active engagement, respect for Pacific priorities and sustained statecraft it took to secure the agreements in the first place — the treaties do not lock anything in.
insights.speaker: Connor Graham
insights.so_what: Implies persistent Australian aid, diplomacy and defence spending in the Pacific is a structural line item, not a one-off investment.
insights.locator: The "permanent contest" for influence in the Pacific does not stop

insights.claim: Taiwan's representative office presence in Port Moresby dated back to 1990, so the closure ends 36 years of continuous unofficial Taiwanese presence in PNG.
insights.speaker: Connor Graham
insights.so_what: Longevity of the office underlines that this is a break in an established norm rather than an incremental adjustment.
insights.locator: a presence dating back to 1990 will end
